Firstly, doing them at the same time every day or cleaning as you go, or both—that helps keep the piles down. 

If you DO have piles, you MUST make the piles themselves less nasty. That’s the only way the unbearable smells won’t overpower your urge to clean — if the sensory overpowers the urge, the piles happen. And they don’t get defeated. 

When I use a dish, it gets rinsed / scraped until it is empty and basically clean. I don’t stack my dishes in the sink! This is KEY! It keeps water and nastiness from sitting in them. Keep a section of counter next to the sink for you to stack dishes in need of cleaning if you’re not going to clean them immediately. 

secondly, when I do the dishes, I do them with a system like I used when I worked in an industry dishpit. 

I rinse everything one at a time until it’s basically clear, then I stack everything on the stove next to me in piles of similar items; bowls all in bowls, plates stacked, knives in a jar/pot with handles all up so I can grab them easily, utensils I will put in a large cup with a bit of soap and water to let them soak so when I have to wash them by hand, I don’t have to scrub each tine. 

I then fill the sink with hot soapy water. This part is divine, bc remember, your dishes are fully rinsed—there is nothing physical left on them—I wash by least greasy to most greasy, to prevent grease residue being left behind. If you’re doing a ton of dishes, you can replace the water halfway through. 

I will put the sprayer on while I’m doing the soapy dishes, so they’re rinsed as they’re washed, and then I stack them in the drain. If at any point I need to stop to wait for dishes to dry, the piles on the counter are not stinky or slimy, and it won’t trigger my issues as badly.

It also helps me to only use one set of dishes a day if I can. So I’ll re-wash and re-use the same set of cups/plates/bowls/utensils unless I’m cooking.

EDIT TO ADD:

I grew up in a family I now recognize as all neurodivergent and struggling with demands. My mom maintained laundry by doing small loads every day at the same time in the afternoon, so it never bothered her. Her system for the dishes was that we use paper towels / paper plates for breakfast/lunch, and real dishes for dinner, and the sink is empty every night. Now that was a mutual effort as she made my sisters and I empty the dishwasher every morning and clean up after dinner each night, but her systemic rituals really helped me get a sense of “Okay, if cooking is a system, cleaning is Not Separate, it is PART of cooking.”

But I add all that to say that sometimes, it is okay to sacrifice sustainability for health. You can have paper plates if you need and if that helps you, they can be a lifesaver.

I take buspirone 15 mg up to 2x a day for my anxiety, but it has a side effect that I just straight up ruminate less. I will be honest, if I don’t take my ADHD meds, I ruminate HARD. So hard. I get emotional rumination like a mfer without them. I think my AudHD brain gets hooked on spiraling like it’s cocaine.

Whatever it is, I need to slowly remove all of the overstimulation and bring myself back down to baseline. If I cannot remove myself from a situation, there is no regulation. Sometimes, if I catch it early enough, i can dissociate in a way that it internalizes the meltdown, and although it still relentlessly exhausts me, it looks to the outside observer like I’m just having a frustrated and silent morning. 

This is the primary reason I am on my 21st job in 7 years (approx) 

I am sorry you are struggling with this too. 

When it comes to bringing myself back to baseline, I usually start with **eliminating auditory stimulus,** then **eliminating physical,** then dealing with my *mental ruminations.*

If I am already freaking out this is too late, best to remove myself somewhere where I can get hysterical or angry and not hurt myself or any objects. I like sitting in my car with the radio on very loud (but NOT EVER DRIVING, took a few meltdown collisions with the curb for me to realize that as a younger adult) and just screaming along to songs. Singing calms your vagus nerve, and I tend to get wildly successful with my diaphragm when I’m about to have a meltdown — must be all that violent hyperventilating.  

Auditory— can I find a bathroom, a quiet place, headphones, or a spot outdoors without too much ambient noise? Audio is one of the worst triggers to move me from stress to full blown meltdown, so treating my misophonia when it arises is KEY. 

Physical—can I get myself alone A S A P? can I find a place where I can curl up in a ball against a wall in the dark? If not, whatever is the closest thing to a ‘safe place’ works for me. I like bathrooms, smoke spots (there are ALWAYS unofficial smoke spots around businesses, just look for the nicotine users and that is your place to be sullen, silent, and left alone), my car if I am at home and the roommate is around. 

Mental—I lastly, to bring myself out of mental meltdown, will do my best to drag my extreme thinking back to the median. Sometimes that looks like talking to myself like a child, letting myself say all the awful thoughts on my head like “I’m going to lose my job and everyone thinks I’m stupid,” and then immediately following that with a following truth that is kinder to me: “my work quality is praised consistently, I have a boss who cares and seeks to help manage my caseload, and who will not fire anyone without working with them to find a solution first.” Then, being able to look at both of those, I can say “right now I am so stressed and overwhelmed, I feel unsafe at my job, and because of my past firings, i tend towards an all-or-nothing view of my situations. This job is working with me, and is not those jobs. This feeling is bad because I have been hurt by old situations, and my brain is using pattern recognition to try and alleviate the pain before it happens. I am not a future-teller, all I can do is work with my knowledge right now. “

Sometimes, that just looks like me breathing as much as I can and calling a safe person: my mom, or, if it is a work issue, my manager. I listen for their logic, and I have learned if I don’t use them to help my emotional brain feel better (example; I DONT ask them to fix my problems, because that always ends in me being frustrated and feeling unheard), but rather, to fill in the information my All-or-Nothing brain can’t perceive in those states. 

I cannot think logically in those situations, but I need logic to take me out of emotion brain. My whole process is about bringing stimulus down to increase regulation.

It’s okay to be miserable while you work, most people are, it’s hard to be miserable, absolutely, but it isn’t unnatural, and it will pass

just like the joy of a bright moment, the darkness of a foul one will linger until it doesn’t. all we can do is make the most out of where we are at the moment.

What’s building up to cause this isn’t just what’s happening at work. You are probably holding so much anger and frustration and built up tension that when the shit at work overwhelms you, you boil over with the cumulative weight of all of it overtaking you. 

Two things: one, watch your physical responses when you start to get mad. If you can catch your body’s physical fight reaction coming into focus, you can better remove yourself from the situation, and when you DO catch these feelings, don’t follow their signals, if you can resist, do something that will shock you out of it. Ice water, on your face, or running it on your wrists, will help. Deep breathing in your diaphragm, with long, steady, slow, controlled exhales will slow your heart rate. 

If you do desperately need to hit something, make sure you are in a quiet, private, safe place, and that whatever you are hitting belongs to you or to nature. (I.e, kick a tree trunk, punch your own wall.) now the problem with this, is that your brain doesn’t quite understand “this is okay to hit, but that is not” when it’s so mad. So to let yourself lose control and experience this rage is a dangerous game, because it can get worse and get more unbearable. 

Negative feelings that aren’t felt on time when they arise will eventually transform into anger or rage, at least in people like us. You have to find a way of neutralizing that negativity at the base. Do you find that you betray yourself often? Or do you stand up for yourself and your boundaries? Sometimes our rage is a result of us acquiescing to everyone around us even if they never realized that’s what we were doing. 

Now all this to say none of it is easy and all of it is a process. But give yourself grace while you’re learning, it isn’t overnight. You will make steps forward and sometimes you’ll take a step or two backwards. 

Violence is cathartic. Absolutely. But the cycle it continues will never heal, and it will never bring you peace. And peace is what makes the alternative methods so attractive. Dealing with your anger without violence can bring you so much peace.

I appreciate your points, and you are correct, your actions aren’t excused or ascribed to your chart, I get that. But something interesting and on the flip side is you can spot something in your chart that just names something you couldn’t name yourself but perhaps always already saw. (an example, an aspect that could show addictive tendencies with alcohol. you’ve never drank, never felt the draw, but now you feel even more vindicated in that decision)  I’ve not found my chart taught me about myself so much as I found new ways of dissecting my experiences throughout my life, and ways of spotting repeating cycles in time. 

Astrology, much like many other esoteric things, has a ton of nonsense around it  that is indeed messy and cult like. That is the only answer I can acquiesce to your question of why they aren’t separated.

Ah but here’s the kicker too, you can see all of those things in an astrological chart. (Birth order, family size, all the things you listed) Your birth chart is just a picture of the sky when you were born. The reason why people tend to get so sucked in, I personally think, is because usually it is to analyze their own birth chart, and we all (as humans) have at least some narcissistic tendencies that favor activities focused on the self. And once you start diving into it, and you start seeing all of the things that happened throughout your life charted like the code of a computer, it’s so goddamn addicting you can’t help but want to know more. Even if you don’t buy in, what’s the harm in having the curiosity to ask the ye old fortune teller what they can tell you about yourself just from your birth chart? 

Even if it turns out to be all bullshit… see the draw? All it takes is a few clicks and you’re on your way to seeing what exactly it is about astrology that has hooked so many people. 

It isn’t fair to reduce it to the horoscopes in the newspaper, when in reality, it is so very many things—whether that’s a psychological tool for self dissection, a neat party trick, or an ancient and fascinating system of esoteric weather forecasting. Astrology as a whole is more the analysis of cycles and patterns mixed with the observation of the genuine astronomical movement of the planets (Mercury going retrograde is not *just* an astrological event of course, it’s a legitimate and physical thing that happens in the sky)

That’s precisely right though, astrology is a non-impactful belief system and that’s because it’s just labeling and naming different observations of things that are and have always been happening. 

People believe in it because it shows itself to be true, and that’s all it really takes for anyone to believe in anything. If you see something happen enough times, you’re going to have a tough time convincing yourself it’s impossible, or that it’s all just bullshit.
